stem.en: A cricket bat costs ₹800 in a sports shop. A student keeps exactly ₹800 in a sealed gullak for a year, and during that year the general level of prices rises by 6%. What is true at the end of the year?

text.en: The ₹800 is now worth about ₹848, because money kept aside grows along with prices.
The ₹800 still buys the bat, because a shop cannot charge more than the price the student saw first.
The ₹800 buys less than a bat, because the bat now costs about ₹848 while the money stayed at ₹800.
The ₹800 buys more than a bat, because a bat that stays unsold in a shop is usually sold cheaper.

explanation.en: Money in a gullak does not grow with prices. 6% of ₹800 is ₹48, so the same bat costs about ₹848 a year later, while the ₹800 is unchanged. The rupees were never lost, but their purchasing power fell: the same ₹800 now covers a little over nine-tenths of the bat.

hints.en: Work out the bat's new price first, then compare it with the ₹800 in the gullak.
The gullak keeps rupees. Purchasing power is about what those rupees can buy.
